T H E  T H E S I S
AI creates output. A-OSP creates reconstructable proof.
The investable point is not a better dashboard. It is owning the evidence object — the open format of proof that 
every other tool will have to read. We are not selling a GRC suite; we are selling the substrate underneath it.
The shift
AI makes producing work faster — and 
reconstructing proof and accountability

reusable evidence: source, lineage,

This round

channel

## Page 6

W H Y  T H E Y  P A Y  N O W
Two clocks force the spend — independent of AI hype
The regulatory clock
• AI Act in force (high-risk Dec 2027); fines up to €35M / 
7% of turnover
• DORA applicable since 17 Jan 2025; NIS2 across 18 
sectors; GDPR already baseline
• Proof is becoming a legal obligation, not a best 
practice
The operational clock
• AI is entering advisory, audit, policy and risk work right 
now
• Output grows faster than verifiability — the 
reconstruction gap widens monthly
• Inference cost falls; trust cost stays high — that spread 
is the margin
The trigger we sell into: an SME facing a 231 update, a NIS2 deadline, a DORA supply-chain request or a first AI-
assisted deliverable under audit. The pain has a date. Public-trust / sovereignty tailwinds (eIDAS 2.0, EUDI) reinforce 
the direction but are not part of this round's sales motion — see appendix.

## Page 14

T H E  I N S T I T U T I O N A L  M O A T
Open standard + company is the moat — not an org chart
It answers three questions at once: why the market trusts it, why incumbents can't own the format, why investors and grants coexist.
Why the market trusts it
A proof format no single vendor 
controls is one an auditor, a DPO or a 
procurement office can rely on. 
Inspectable beats proprietary where 
evidence is the product.
Why incumbents can't own 
it
An incumbent can copy features into 
its suite. It cannot retroactively own an 
open, neutral format already adopted 
by associations and held by a 
foundation.
Why capital types coexist
The non-profit attracts grants and 
public money; the OpCo attracts 
equity. Each funds what it should —
neither contaminates the other's 
incentives.
The standard ambition belongs here, not in the revenue line. A-OSP does not need to sell to governments to be valuable —
but to become respectable, neutral and adoptable as a format, the open core and a credible standards body are the 
mechanism. That is why the legal architecture is strategy, not paperwork. (Where it sells — PA, sovereign, model makers —
stays in the appendix; why it can become a standard stays here.)

## Page 15

I P  &  V A L U E  C A P T U R E
Who owns what. How the OpCo makes money if the core is 
open
Foundation owns
• The open specification of the evidence format (the 
standard)
• The trademark and the certification mark («A-OSP-
compliant»)
• Open-core reference implementation, under a network-
copyleft licence
• Neutral governance of the spec via a standards 
committee
OpCo owns
• All product IP: enterprise modules, managed runtime, 
integrations
• A durable commercial licence to the core for paid 
services and deployments
• The brand for commercial offerings; customer contracts 
and data-processing
• Equity, ESOP, the cap table — what investors actually 
buy
How the OpCo captures value while the core stays open
• Open core = trust and distribution; the things buyers actually pay for are NOT in the commons: SLAs, managed hosting, 
enterprise lenses, certifications, sovereign deployments, support
• The certification mark is the toll: «A-OSP-compliant» is granted by the Foundation but operationalized through OpCo tooling 
and services
• Investor neutrality concern resolved: the Foundation governs the spec (independent board); the OpCo cannot unilaterally fork 
the standard — which is precisely what makes the standard credible and therefore valuable
